items.prompt: White to move. Find checkmate in one.
hints: Look at where the enemy king stands. Which squares can it reach, and which are covered by your pieces?
A checkmate needs a check that leaves the king no square to go to. Your own king helps by covering squares.
Try each check in turn: can the king step away, or capture the checking piece?
items.explain: Qf8# is checkmate: it gives check and the enemy king has no legal reply.

items.prompt: White to move. Checkmate in two: find the first move.
hints: There is no mate in one. You need a first move that takes away squares or confines the king.
After your move the enemy king must move. Ask: whatever it does, can you mate next move?
Prefer quiet moves that keep the king boxed in; checks are not always the best first step.
items.explain: Ka6, Kb6 and Kc6 each force checkmate on the next move whatever the enemy king does.

hints: Before you move, ask what the enemy king will be able to do afterwards.
A king that is not attacked and has no legal move is stalemate: the game is drawn. Leave the king a move, or mate it.
Count the squares next to the enemy king after your move: is at least one free, or is the king mated?
items.explain: Qh2# is checkmate. Careful: Qa7 and Qb1 would stalemate the enemy king and only draw (tablebase: draw).

items.prompt: Black to move and has no legal move. Is this checkmate or stalemate?

hints: Is the king attacked right now?
A king that is attacked with no escape is checkmated. A king that is not attacked but cannot move (and nothing else can move) is stalemated.
Look at every square next to the king and at the lines of the enemy pieces.
items.explain: The king is not attacked but the side to move has no legal move: stalemate, which is a draw.
